TEXTILE calculates the development of a 3D-curved surface. It includes the compentation of the stressed membrane to obtain the cutting pattern areas.

Necessary precondition for a cutting pattern is the formfinding. The formfinding has to create a stressed system in equilibrium. In this step, different prestress definitions will produce different membrane forms.
Figure 2.1: Formfinding: on the left folded input system, on the rigth stressed membrane

The membrane shall be cut at so called geodetic lines. Geodetic lines are the shortest connec- tion of two points on a curved surface. Definition and analysis of these geodetic lines is done in the program WINGRAF.
The definition of the cutting lines in the groundview can be done in 3 ways:
1. With an ASCII definition in PROG TEXTILE see example textile1_tennishall.dat

On problems in creating cutting areas please notice:
1. Best define cuttinglines in the ground view

2. In case cuttinglines have a kink or attach other cuttinglines inside the membranne best use a polygon (the cuttinglines should be defined in a sequence one after the other and should not come unsorted)
cuttinglines shall go a little bit over the boundary (define them a longer)
The geodetic lines define the cutting areas in the 3D space. The cutting areas are determined and numbered in the program WINGRAF:
Figure 2.3: 3D-cutting areas: shown in a ground view

Now the 3D cutting areas have to be developed into a 2D plane. This is the main task of TEXTILE. This ironing or polishing will cause additional strains and stresses in the material. These stresses depend on the shear stiffness of the textile material. Without shear stiffness nearly every 3D surface can be developed into plane by creating rhombus meshes. Now the sense of the geodetic lines appears: an area defined with geodetic lines can be developed as a rather straight area, although it appears like a curved banana in 3D (areas in the left lower region of the previous picture).
Figure 2.4: Plane 2D cutting areas, dashed = stressed form, filled region = relaxed form
In this picture the cutting areas are moved in plane as in an explosion plot to avoid overlapping. The explosion factor can be adjusted in WINGRAF.

Zur Kontrolle der Abwicklung druckt TEXTILE in einer Textausgabe die Fläche der ur- sprünglichen 3-D- Zuschnittsflächen sowie die Flächen der glattgebügelten 2-D-Gebiete sowie der entspannten Membranfläche aus. Man erkennt, dass die 2D-Fläche genauso groß ist wie die ursprüngliche räumliche 3D-Fläche, die entspannte Fläche aber kleiner ist: TEXTILE prints the areas of the original 3D surface as well as the ironed 2D area and the relaxed cutting area. The ironed 2D must have the same area as the original 3D surface, the relaxed cutting area is smaller:

With a test storage the pressing down of the 3D area into plane can be well animated, see example textile_animation.dat -> Animator loadcase 1001:
Figure 2.5: Pressing down the 3D area into plane (first left cutting area)
In the relaxation step, the material shrinks to a stressfree area. As a textile has a huge nonlin- ear material behaviour, different compensation methods are available in program TEXTILE:
1. Without further input the material shrinks according to the prestress and the linear material parameters.
2. Independant of the prestress a constant compensation strain can be defined in warp and fill direction.
3. 1+2: In addition to the linear material prestress strain an additive compensation strain can be defined.
For the elastic prestress strain, separate material parameters can be set.

5. For stress relations N-warp/N-fill the compenstion matrix can be defined. According to the actual stress in the current finite element a warp/fill compenstion strain eps- warp/eps-fill can be computed. With these matrix input the nonlinear behaviour of the compensation can be solved exactly.

Near the boundary cables and at the seam lines not the full compensation of the undistorted textile can be taken into account. One reason is, that in practice it is often not possible to stress the membrane tangetial to the stressed stiff boundary cable. Another reason is the higher stiffness at the seam lines.
This effect called decompensation must be equalized by adding material at the end of the cloth width. This is the reason why always both the stressed and the stressfree 2D areas are plotted!

With CUTT DECO... DECL... a linear decreasing relaxation in fill direction can be defined on the last DECL meters of the cutting areas. The region can be plotted in WINGRAF via ”structure of 2D-cutting areas”. Example: compare created areas with/without DECO in tex- tile4_cutting_via_elements.dat).
Figure 2.6: Magenta=stressed, green=relaxed. left without DECO, right with DECO
But DECO has only little effect if EDGE>=0 is used. EDGE can control the edge length much more effective. Then DECO has only an effect on the inner membrane area (beside the edge).
Default is EDGE 0.50. Then the flattened edge has just the same length as in the 3D system. After the compensation it gets a bit shorter due to the reduced compensation (factor 0.5).
For the development of surface and the compensation the definition of the warp direction is very important. For this reason different methods to describe warp direction are available in TEXTILE:
1. By default the program calculates the principal axis for the 2D cutting area and sets the warp direction into the longer axis.

2. If the 2D-area is ”compact” and no clear principal axis can be extracted, the program takes the average of the original finite element coordination systems. This averaged local x axis will then be taken as warp direction for all elements of this cutting area.
For special purpose a fixed angle in X-Y space can be defined for each cutting area.
In the current sample the default had been used. The warp direction can be plotted with a red line in WINGRAF:

The input is made in the CADINP language (see general manual SOFiSTiK: ’FEA / STRUC- TURAL Installation and Basics’). Three categories of units are distinguished:
mm Fixed unit. Input is always required in the specified unit.
[mm] Explicit unit. Input defaults to the specified unit. Alternatively, an explicit as- signment of a related unit is possible (eg. 2.5[m] ).

[mm]1011 Implicit unit. Implicit units are categorised semantically and denoted by a cor- responding identity number (shown in green). Valid categories referring to the unit ”length” are, for example, geodetic elevation, section length and thickness. The default unit for each category is defined by the currently active (design code specific) unit set. This input default can be overridden as described above. The specified unit in square brackets corresponds to the default for unit set 5 (Eu- rocodes, NORM UNIT 5).

Standard input using cutting area definition of WINGRAF:

HEAD Cutting analysis - development of surface + compensation cutting $ Cutting analysis with cutting area definition of WINGRAF $ Realistic compensation added to elastic material strain in percent: COMP DE1 - 0.5 $ Percent additional strain in warp direction COMP DE2 - 1.5 $ Percent additional strain in fill direction END
1. Definition of the cutting areas in WINGRAF:
Then in TEXTILE usually only the input CUTT is sufficient. The cutting areas as well as the load case for the compensation is taken from WINGRAF.
Only if additional input for MNO, LOCX or PROJ shall be made, these parameters may be input using the number of the cutting area NO. The first CUTT input line is taken as default for all other areas.
2. Manual definition of the cutting areas via groups:
If one ore more groups are activated via GRP, the cutting areas are not taken from WINGRAF. The compensation load case has to be defined.
defines cutting area 3 consisting of membrane elements of groups 3,4 and 5.
If no input is done for NO, the cutting area gets the number of the first activated group.
The input CUTT NO -1 deletes all existing cutting areas in the database if the area numbering shall be changed.
LOCX: By default the program calculates the principal axis for each 2D cutting area and sets the warp direction into the longer axis.

If the 2D-area is "compact" and no clear principal axis can be extracted, the program takes the average of the original finite element coordination systems. This averaged local x axis will then be taken as warp direction for all elements of this cutting area.
For speccial purpose a fixed angle in X-Y space can be defined for each cutting area.

PROJ: In extreme special cases the program cannot find a projection direction to flash all elements on the surface. Then a projection direction can be defined manually - please refer to sample m_eck3.dat.

EDGE: If you take an orange slice and press it onto the table, the outer edges will expand and will get longer. The same happens in TEXTILE with EDGE=-1 on a double curved cutting area. But usually you want to attach the membrane to a boundary with a fixed length - so the edges shall not get longer. This you get with EDGE>=0. Then the edges keep their length but as
an effect the flattened area gets a bit smaller as the edges must be compressed a bit (orange slice).

With a factor between 0 and 1 you can control the compensation at the edge (from the stress). In most cases you have double material at the edge and/or a boundary cable that prohibits a strain in edge direction. With EDGE you can control this compensation at the edge. With EDGE=0.0 the relaxed length will be as long as the stressed length - it will be the length that you measure in the 3D system. With EDGE=1.0 the edge gets the full compensation and the relaxed length will be shorter. But then during the erection you must stress and elongate the edge what usually causes problems.

Effect of EDGE see example textile7_edge.dat : EDGE=-1.0 cannot be installed - edge cannot be compressed EDGE=0.00 edge must not be stressed during montage EDGE=0.30 edge must be stressed a bit during montage = possible EDGE=1.00 edge must be stressed very high in the montage = problematic

EXPO: To avoid an overlapping of the cutting areas in the graphical plots, the areas are moved horizontally in the 2D plane as in an explosion plot. The explosion factor can also be adjusted in WINGRAF.

There are different possibilities to describe the compensation:
1. Without an input COMP the material shrinks according to the prestress and the linear material parameters, perhaps with a material property which is input separately via CUTT-MNO.
2. Independant of the prestress a constant compensation strain can be defined in warp and fill direction.
COMP CE1 - 2.0 $ 2 % constant strain in warp direction COMP CE2 - 5.0 $ 5 % constant strain in fill direction
3. 1+2: In addition to the linear material prestress strain an additive compensation strain can be defined.
COMP DE1 - 2.0 $ 2 % additional strain in warp direction
COMP DE2 - 5.0 $ 5 % additional strain in fill direction

4. For stress relations N-warp/N-fill the compenstion matrix can be defined. According to the actual stress in the current finite element a warp/fill compenstion strain eps- warp/eps-fill can be computed. With these matrix input the nonlinear behaviour of the compensation can be solved exactly:
COMP S1 4 0.00 1.00 4.00 10.00 $ warp (warp direction) COMP S2 4 0.00 1.00 4.00 10.00 $ fill (fill direction)
COMP E1 1 3.0 4.0 4.5 5.0 $ warp (warp direction) COMP E1 2 2.0 3.2 3.6 4.3

If a point has a membrane force of 10 kN/m in warp direction and of 4 kN/m in fill direction, the compensation strain results as follows:
Column=4 follows due to 10 kN/m warp force
Line=3 follows due to 4 kN/m fill force (because COMP S2...W3=4)

Usually the cutting lines are defined interactively in WINGRAF or SOFIPLUS. But they can also be defined in a batch run with this record LINE. A following WINGRAF run takes these cutting lines, calculates the geodetic lines and computes the 3D-cutting areas. Please also refer to example 1+2.
TYPE GEOD lines create a geodetic line with the shortest connnection on the surface, TYPE FIX linies are restraint lines and remain straight in the ground view.

In file textile1.dat a plane input system is blown up with a constant inner air pressure. The second formfinding step is very important for this example because the inner air pressure has to get the right load direction vertical to the deformed shape! The program computes the load on the system defined with the primary load case! So in load case 2 the loadvector is computed with the deformed mesh of primary load case 1! In the first step of load case 1 the load is applied only in vertical z direction of the original plane mesh! Thus the deformed mesh of load case 2 slightly varies from the deformed mesh of load case 1:
Figure 4.2: Formfinding load case 1 (load direction global z)
Figure 4.3: Formfinding load case 2 (air pressure on deformed shape LC 1)
For further analysis it is very comfortable to show new deformations starting at the formfinding position. Therefore it is necessary to make a system update:
prog ase head Coordinate-Update syst PLC 2 STOR yes end

With this run, the nodal coordinates are moved to the deformed position of load case 2. Staring the animator now, at once the formfinding geometry is shown as new undeformed system. A plot in WINGRAF shows the system with the new element coordinate systems:
Figure 4.4: After the system update: new local coordiante systems

Now all real static load cases can be computed. It is important to define load case 2 as the primary load case because this load case includes the formfinding prestress of all elements. Furthermore all active elements must be taken into account with a group stiffness factor of 1.0. The following input shows a simplified input of a windloading:
HEAD Wind with 1.0 stiffness syst prob th3 nmat yes PLC 2 lc 11 titl ’Wind in x’ LC 901,902 end
Figure 4.5: Deformation due to wind loading

Now the cutting pattern analysis can be done. Usually the cutting lines are defined interactively in WINGRAF or SOFIPLUS. In this example they are defined in an extra TEXTILE batch run. A following WINGRAF run takes these cutting lines, calculates the geodetic lines and computes, stores and plots the 3D-cutting areas.
Figure 4.6: geodetic lines in ground view
Figure 4.7: Geodetic lines in a 3D plot

Now all necessary data is available for the cutting pattern in TEXTILE. At first the development of surface produces the stressed 2D-area in the XY-plane (plotted in dashed lines). The strips shrink due to the compensation method and lead to the final stressfree cutting pattern area - area after compensation (plotted in unbroken lines or filled area)

The output listing shows the 7 areas. The following warning appears because in the input system the local element x coordinates point to global X while the strips are oriented in global Y. You could avoid this by rotating the local x axis of the elements to global Y.
